This chapter explains what the four learners share, where they differ and which hyperparameters they take. Every learner predicts one penalty, `log(lambda)`, per sequence.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3changepoint)
library(data.table)
```

## The shared pipeline

All four learners train the same way up to the regressor.

1. Features. `penaltyLearning::featureVector()` summarises each sequence as a numeric vector: its length and statistics such as quantiles and variance estimates of the signal and its differences. Training drops columns that are not finite or are constant, and prediction uses the same columns.
2. Model path. For each sequence, a solver fits the best model of each complexity up to `Kmax`. Changepoint tasks use `changepoint::cpt.mean(method = "SegNeigh")`, which minimises the square loss for 0 to `Kmax` changes. Peak tasks use `PeakSegOptimal::PeakSegPDPAchrom()`, which minimises the Poisson loss for 0 to `Kmax` peaks.
3. Model selection. `penaltyLearning::modelSelection()` finds the range of `log(lambda)` over which each model is selected.
4. Label errors. `penaltyLearning::labelError()` for changepoint labels, or `PeakError::PeakError()` for peak labels, counts the false positives and false negatives of each model.
5. Target intervals. `penaltyLearning::targetIntervals()` gives each sequence the interval of `log(lambda)` values with the fewest label errors. One end of the interval may be infinite.
6. Regression. The regressor maps the features to the target intervals.

At prediction time, the learner computes the same features and returns the regressor's `log(lambda)`. The measures and `autoplot()` rebuild the model path and pick the model that penalty selects.

## The four learners

| Learner | Regressor | Package |
|---------|-----------|---------|
| `changepoint.intregrcv` | Linear model with L1 regularisation and a squared hinge loss on the intervals, with the regularisation chosen by cross-validation | penaltyLearning |
| `changepoint.xgboost.aft` | Gradient boosted trees with the accelerated failure time loss for interval-censored targets | xgboost |
| `changepoint.mmit` | Maximum margin interval tree | mmit |
| `changepoint.mmif` | Forest of maximum margin interval trees grown on bootstrap samples and random feature subsets | mmit |

`changepoint.featureless` is a baseline that skips the features and the regressor. It predicts the one constant `log(lambda)` with the fewest label errors summed over the training sequences, so a learner above is only worth its features if it beats this baseline.

The linear model needs training labels that give at least one finite lower limit and at least one finite upper limit. Without them it stops with an error. The three tree-based learners train as long as one limit is finite.

## Hyperparameters

Every learner requires `Kmax`. It caps model complexity: the largest number of changes (changepoint labels) or peaks (peak labels) on each model path, at training and at prediction. A penalty that would select a more complex model selects the `Kmax` model instead. Set it at least as large as the number of changes a labelled sequence needs. A larger `Kmax` makes each path slower to compute.

| Learner | Other hyperparameters |
|---------|-----------------------|
| `changepoint.intregrcv` | `n.folds`, `min.observations`, `reg.type`, `initial.regularization`, `factor.regularization`, `margin.vec`, `verbose` |
| `changepoint.xgboost.aft` | `nrounds` (100), `eta`, `max_depth`, `min_child_weight`, `aft_loss_distribution`, `aft_loss_distribution_scale`, `nthread` (1) |
| `changepoint.mmit` | `max_depth`, `margin` |
| `changepoint.mmif` | `max_depth`, `margin`, `n_trees`, `n_features` |
| `changepoint.featureless` | none |

Each learner's reference page links to the function it wraps, which documents these. The parameter set lists them too.

```{r}
lrn("changepoint.xgboost.aft")$param_set$ids()
```

## Predictions record Kmax

A predicted penalty only makes sense with the model path it was learned on. Each prediction therefore records `Kmax` for every sequence in its extra data. The measures read it from there, which keeps scores right after `resample()`, inside an `AutoTuner` and in a `GraphLearner`.

## Side by side

The toy task has ten sequences. The odd ones change mean twice and carry two `1change` labels, and the even ones are flat with one `0changes` label.

```{r}
set.seed(36)
signal = vector("list", 10L)
label = vector("list", 10L)
for (i in seq_len(10L)) {
  if (i %% 2L == 1L) {
    signal[[i]] = c(rnorm(100, 18), rnorm(100, 36), rnorm(100, 9))
    label[[i]] = data.table(start = c(90, 190), end = c(110, 210), label = "1change")
  } else {
    signal[[i]] = rnorm(100, 0)
    label[[i]] = data.table(start = 1, end = 100, label = "0changes")
  }
}
task = TaskCpt$new(
  id = "toy", backend = data.table(signal = signal, label = label),
  target = "label", sequence = "signal", label_type = "changepoint"
)
```

The MMIT and MMIF learners need the mmit package, so this chunk adds them only when it is installed.

```{r}
learners = list(
  lrn("changepoint.intregrcv", Kmax = 3L, n.folds = 2L, min.observations = 2L),
  lrn("changepoint.xgboost.aft", Kmax = 3L)
)
if (requireNamespace("mmit", quietly = TRUE)) {
  learners = c(learners, lrns(c("changepoint.mmit", "changepoint.mmif"), Kmax = 3L))
}
```

Each learner trains on the task and predicts on it. The table has one column of predicted `log(lambda)` per learner.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
predictions = list()
response = data.table(row_id = task$row_ids)
for (learner in learners) {
  predictions[[learner$id]] = learner$train(task)$predict(task)
  response[[learner$id]] = round(predictions[[learner$id]]$response, 2)
}
response
```

The penalties differ between learners, but each one only has to fall inside its sequence's target interval. The label error shows which ones do.

```{r}
errors = numeric()
for (id in names(predictions)) {
  errors[id] = predictions[[id]]$score(msr("changepoint.label_error"), task = task)
}
errors
```

To add a learner, inherit from [`LearnerCpt`](../reference/LearnerCpt.html) and return a `log(lambda)` per sequence, with `Kmax` in the extra data.
